#25235. Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (684 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Why electrification is the climate game changer we need

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas.
  • Recent findings suggest that if fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
  • According to recent reports, in a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

Recent findings suggest that if fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels. That is according to a recent analysis by the International Energy Agency, which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.

According to recent reports, in a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

In a recent development, but the way the electricity running these things is generated is also vital. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.

Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.

Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.

It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.

In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

The World Resources Institute, an independent research organization, recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

Recent findings suggest that A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.

It has been revealed that as electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity and electrified demand.

According to the International Energy Agency, annual grid investment has to increase by about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (five to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (one to five years), and EV charging infrastructure (one to two years).

Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

By CALUM CROWE, SCOTTISH DEPUTY CHIEF SPORTS WRITER.

Published: 14:13 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:26 EST, 17 November 2026.

Of all the many stories written by F Scott Fitzgerald, one of the finest authors and wordsmiths of his time, The Great Gatsby will forever remain his masterpiece.

In some of his other work written as he travelled across Europe, Fitzgerald also had a line about Switzerland, describing it as a ‘country where very few things begin, but many things end.’.

It is a curious quote and, like much of Fitzgerald’s work, is open to interpretation. As the man who also wrote The Curious Case of Benjamin Button, curiosity was a common theme.

As for the Curious Case of Sebastien Pocognoli, Switzerland may, indeed, be the country where everything came to an end.

What unfolded in St Gallen on Monday evening was a horror show. Scotland were battered 4-0 by Switzerland’s B team. There is no way to sugar-coat a result like that, no way to dress it up as anything other than an embarrassment. They played OK for half an hour and then fell apart.

Pocognoli claimed afterwards that there were positives to be taken and how some of Scotland’s football was the best they have produced across his six matches in charge.

Sebastien Pocognoli is facing serious questions after a miserable Nations League campaign.

Utter nonsense. That was a manager clutching at straws at the end of a Nations League campaign which has been an unmitigated disaster pretty much from start to finish.

Let’s go back to the very start here. After Steve Clarke had pushed the Scottish Football Association (SFA) into awarding him a upcoming four-year contract, only to then walk away after the World Cup, it was a chance for a fresh start.

On the day when Pocognoli was unveiled as the new head coach in August, Ian Maxwell and Craig Mulholland, the SFA’s chief executive and chief football officer, were beaming with positivity.

They told us all how data and AI had been used in the recruitment process, and how several clubs across Europe had been chasing Pocognoli.

They clearly viewed it as a coup to have landed the 39-year-old Belgian, who had won a league title in his homeland with Union Saint-Gilloise before a short stint with Monaco.

What would the data say now? Six games played, two wins, a draw and three defeats, five goals scored and ten conceded, seven points and a lousy third-placed finish in Group B1.

It has been revealed that both of those wins came against a North Macedonian side who lost all six of their games. They were a pub team – and Scotland still struggled to beat them at Hampden last Friday night.

Pocognoli was unable to inspire any resistance as his side succumbed to defeat in St Gallen.

Industry observers note that scotland lost 7-0 on aggregate to Switzerland over the two games. Against Slovenia, a 0-0 draw on the opening day in Ljubljana was then followed with a woeful 2-1 defeat at Hampden.

All of which begs a very simple question. Where, exactly, are the grounds for optimism here? How is this getting any better?

When Pocognoli arrived, he spoke about trying to change the style of play, get Scotland playing a more exciting brand of football, whilst bringing through a fresh generation of players.

It was not a rebuild. He inherited a group of players who were accustomed to success under Clarke and who qualified for three tournaments out of a possible four.

His remit was to help Scotland take the next step in major tournaments. With a more dynamic style of play, the job was to help the nation take the next step.

It has been revealed that there has been no revolution thus far. No evidence whatsoever that this coach is capable of delivering results nor a better style of play.

It has been revealed that there is no satisfaction to be taken in any of this. When Pocognoli was appointed, it was, in the eyes of this observer, an interesting and progressive move.

SFA chiefs Craig Mulholland and Ian Maxwell proudly unveil newly introduced boss Pocognoli at Hampden.

Industry observers note that over the past 48 hours or so, there has been a lot of revisionism from some folk about Clarke. ‘Aye, the grass isn’t always greener...’.

That’s garbage. Clarke’s time was up with Scotland. He should never have been handed a new four-year deal in the first place. At least he did the right thing in resigning after the World Cup.

Sources indicate that the whole thing was finished. The problem is that the SFA look like they have appointed a total dud as his successor. Both of those things can be true at the same time.

It is also worth remembering that the only reason we arrived at Pocognoli is because Clarke walked away. The SFA did not instigate any change.

The hiring of a latest head coach was not a proactive change of direction, but a reactive move from an executive body who became accepting of Clarke’s limitations and allowed him to position them over a barrel.

Sources indicate that listen, there is nothing inherently wrong with using data and metrics in football. It’s the modern way. Using data to inform decisions and recruitment processes is smart business.

Recent findings suggest that but the data in itself is no guarantee of success. There are some intangibles in football, things which are harder to quantify. Like a manager who blindly sticks to a system which is patently ill-suited to the players at his disposal.

Industry observers note that things like leadership and communication skills. We can cut Pocognoli some slack in that English is not his first language. He comes across as a thoroughly decent and likeable chap. He’s doing his best. He wants to embrace the culture and makes an effort to sing the National Anthem.

Scotland's defeat arose from individual mistakes, a common theme during the Belgian's reign.

According to recent reports, all of that is undoubtedly to be welcomed. Good on him. But would anyone describe him as an inspirational figure?

When you listen to him speak, have you ever felt slightly confused in terms of the message he’s actually trying to get across?

How must that sound in the dressing room? When Andy Robertson spoke post-match on Monday night, there was frustration in his voice.

The captain insisted there is simply no time or patience with these things. Scotland need to deliver results now.

To be fair, there actually would be a degree of patience shown by the Tartan Army towards Pocognoli if there was something to actually believe in.

According to recent reports, there was a lot of goodwill towards him at the start. If there were signs across these last six games that he could deliver a more exciting team to watch, they would show patience.

Recent findings suggest that but on the basis of what we’ve seen so far, there’s been absolutely nothing to suggest he can move this team forward. Ask yourself a very simple question – do Scotland pass the eye test?

Are we seeing a team who are playing on the front foot and creating chances? The answer, obviously, is no.

According to recent reports, steve Clarke celebrates Scotland's win over Denmark a year ago... how fans miss such highs.

Many Scotland fans are now confronting the possibility that we might not even qualify for Euro 2028, a tournament which we are co-hosting.

By finishing third in the Nations League, we will now be in pot three for the Euro qualifiers and will face a more difficult group.

Beyond that, we would be relying on the back-door method of one of the best-placed home nations not to qualify directly.

Industry observers note that those Euro qualifiers will start in March of next year. Does Pocognoli even make it that far? Or should the SFA hold their hands up, admit they’ve made a mistake, and rectify it?

According to recent reports, that feels unlikely. But on the basis of what we have seen over these first six games, it’s hard to see how this gets any better.

In a recent development, we are worse now than we were at the end under Clarke. Much, much worse. This is not teething problems. It’s a team who have regressed massively under a head coach who was supposed to move the whole thing forward.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Projections of future climate change show a relatively cooler world thanks to the growth of renewable energy. And yet the world is still on track to reach around 2.6˚C of warming by the end of the century — far beyond what many climate scientists say we need to avoid the worst impacts of climate change. So, what are we going to do about it?

In the second episode of Cooked? I talk to experts around the world about their substantial ideas of what we can do to tackle climate change. We talk about energy, food, economics and how the world needs to adapt to a warmer world.

00:00 How can we save the world?

04:27 The synergistic solutions to climate change and other substantial challenges.

12:03 Can we end humanity’s addiction to meat?

21:49 How to make economics work to fight climate change.

33:30 Why the world needs to adapt.

How countries can grow without impoverishing future generations.

Nick Petrić Howe: And then one final question, super easy one, what do we need to do to save the world?

Hannah Ritchie: Haha, oh that’s a tough one.

Sources indicate that nick Petrić Howe: When it comes to climate, there’s one thing that’s been on my mind for a long time. What are we supposed to do about it? Saving the world isn’t quite as easy as it looks in movies. You can’t just blow-up climate change and then walk coolly off into the distance.

But after the last episode of this series, it did feel like things were a bit more positive than I had previously thought. Renewable energy and electrification are making a dent in our emissions. But, the other thing that was clear was that simply relying on renewables won’t be enough and even that progress needs to move more promptly. So, I was interested in some of the massive ideas that are out there. What other ways can we well… save the world?

So, I asked a lot of different experts that exact question. Their answers ranged from the nuanced...

Eoin McLaughlin: What do we want to achieve, right? Is ultimately what the question should be. Is like, well, what kind of society do we want to have? Do we want to have one that is, you know, prosperous in the future? Or do we just want to focus on what's going on day-to-day within the political cycle.

It has been revealed that nick Petrić Howe: In fairness, I didn't actually expect an answer. If there were easy answers, we’d have done it already. Silver bullets are great for werewolves, but they rarely exist for huge global issues. But that didn’t stop me from wanting to know what we should do.

Sources indicate that I'm Nick Petrić Howe and this is Cooked? a podcast miniseries for Nature where I try and figure out whether there's still hope in the battle against climate change or whether we're well… cooked.

According to recent reports, in this episode, I'm going to try and find out some of the big ideas to try and counter climate change. And I knew exactly where to start.

Hannah Ritchie: What I wanted to do is to look at the data and understand if we want to solve these problems, what are the really key and big things that we need to do to solve them?

Nick Petrić Howe: If you tuned into the previous episode, you’ll know that I was feeling pretty down about the climate. To my mind, not enough was being done and what was being done wasn’t going far enough. So I kinda was wondering if we’re well… a bit fucked?

In a recent development, but I learnt last time that maybe I was being a bit pessimistic. And one of the people I spoke to had a lot to say on this, along with a lot of data to back themselves up. It turned out they also had some massive ideas to go along with this.

According to recent reports, hannah Ritchie: Humans actually are capable of solving problems when we put resources behind it, where we really get our act together and work on it. And that obviously has spillovers for climate. you know, I think it is possible for us to tackle this.

Nick Petrić Howe: This is Hannah Ritchie, who you may remember from the last episode. She is a data scientist at Our World in Data and the University of Oxford and has written a book about how we can solve seven key environmental problems, including climate change.

Like the quotes from the start, there are nuanced or simplistic ways to think about solving climate change. On the face of it all that we need to do is stop emitting carbon. That is obviously not quite so straightforward, especially because... climate change isn’t the only problem we have.

Recent findings suggest that climate change regularly comes up in polls as a big concern, but when compared to other complications people tend to be more anxious about more immediate worries, like the cost of living, the economy and crime. With only finite resources and energy, climate change can fade into the background.

But by looking at the data, Hannah has found that there are ways to tackle climate change and other issues.

It has been revealed that hannah Ritchie: So, if you take the example of climate change and air pollution, the root of basically both of those problems is burning stuff, right? And either that's burning wood or biomass, so indoor air pollution is still a huge glitch for people and actually is linked to energy poverty. So millions of people still die from indoor air pollution or outdoor air pollution — basically the burning of fossil fuels. The core solution there is to basically move away from burning stuff and primarily burning fossil fuels. Increasingly we have good alternatives, low-carbon and cleaner alternatives to these sources.

Nick Petrić Howe: This isn’t to say there aren’t trade-offs to any particular solution, there are still potential downsides that would need to be managed, but the point is that there are ways to tackle climate change and tackle other problems people care about.

In a recent development, to take the example of air pollution, one key outdoor pollutant is sulphur dioxide; this primarily gets in the air from burning of oil or coal and can make it hard to breathe. So, using less oil or coal can reduce this kind of air pollution and benefit the climate. Billions of people worldwide are also exposed to indoor air pollution, which comes from burning of wood, kerosene or coal indoors. A shift to electric or gas heating and cooking would also make people’s homes healthier and send fewer warming emissions out into the world.

Sources indicate that transitions, though, can be tricky. In China, for example, in an effort to reduce air pollution, using coal has been banned in some places, even though some people can’t afford the alternatives, like gas heating.

At the societal level, this would still benefit people’s health and the climate, and alternatives would come down in price. And Hannah thinks that the data can guide us towards the decisions that may bring the most benefits. But she also cautions against looking for the ‘perfect solution’.

Hannah Ritchie: So, I think it's often the case that when we're thinking about any of the alternatives to the current system we have, whether that's solar power or wind or electric vehicles or plant-based substitutes, I think we often have this challenge that we're on the hunt for the ultimate solution that has zero downsides, right? And by zero downsides, I mean, you don't need no mining for it. The land-use is very low or basically zero. There are zero repercussions or knock-on impacts whatsoever. And think the reality is if that's the kind of solution that we're waiting for to appear, it's not going to. And the reality is that that stops us actually moving forward and taking action because we're waiting for it. And the reality is we'll just wait on a current system which is mostly running on fossil fuels.

It has been revealed that nick Petrić Howe: You can see this kind of thinking play out with electric cars. People who are passionate about tackling climate change and those that are against it both can come up with reasons to decry electric vehicles. They’ll point to the damage of mining the lithium required for the batteries, that public transport is better for the environment than any personal vehicle, or that buying an old combustion engine car avoids the emissions of manufacturing a fresh electric one. And there are merits to some of these arguments, and things that should be addressed. Public transport could be improved and that would have big climate benefits, mining should be done in the least environmentally damaging way, and there are emissions involved in making a new car. But when it comes down to it, in the long-term electric cars are far better for the climate than regular cars. To Hannah’s point before, they also help reduce air pollution. And we live in a world where cars are integral to many people’s lives, so if people need to drive isn’t a better alternative, better than no alternative?

Hannah also thinks that making viable alternatives for people is going to key in the fight against climate change.

Hannah Ritchie: We could sit here and say well people should just do this because they should just care about the climate and reducing their emissions. And I think lots of people do have that motivation but I think we also need to engage with the fact that people make decisions based on other factors or actually are limited by other factors. Nick Petrić Howe: For those of you that tuned into the previous episode, you’ll know that one of the biggest reasons for optimism when it comes to climate change is due to the energy transition — people using more renewable energy. And the reason for that is that it’s a cheaper alternative to fossil fuels. But it underlines Hannah’s point — that when there is a better, and cheaper, alternative available people will use it.

This could also speak to the synergies that Hannah talked about. Cheap, renewable energy could also lift many people out of poverty and could provide power locally, rather than relying on expensive imports of fossil fuels.

Industry observers note that and this was one of the most positive aspects of Hannah’s book to me. In the past, I’d always kinda assumed that if we want to improve people’s lives across the world, eliminating poverty and giving people access to all the luxuries I see as commonplace, we’d need to rely on fossil fuels to a certain extent. Hannah Ritchie: I don't think that's as much of a dilemma anymore. We do not need to build out energy and provide people with energy services and the positive things that that brings with fossil fuels anymore. We have viable, affordable, increasingly good alternatives to that.

According to recent reports, nick Petrić Howe: You can see this playing out right now in India. And across Africa, where many people live on under a dollar a day, clean energy investments have doubled in recent years, as policies increasing look to make renewable energy part of the mix. Trends which are set to continue as prices for renewable energy keep falling.

It has been revealed that nick Petrić Howe: None of this is exactly straightforward, but what I got from my conversation with Hannah is that there are solutions out there and by looking at the data we can find ways to solve some of them at the same time. Rather than 100 solutions for a hundred problems, maybe we can find a few solutions that meet a few goals at once.

And part of that will involve creating alternatives that people actually want and can make their lives better. Renewable energy makes sense for a lot of people, especially as costs have tumbled.

It has been revealed that and Hannah was pretty optimistic overall. Even after spending years looking at the, sometimes bleak, data on climate, she does believe that we can create a better and more sustainable world. There was one aspect, that often comes up in discussions of climate, that she was a bit more pessimistic about.

Hannah Ritchie: I'm relatively sceptical that large amounts of people shift to a more plant-based diet.

Nick Petrić Howe: But perhaps there’s a lesson from renewable energy here too.

Bruce Friedrich: About a decade ago, it occurred to me and others that we could take a page from energy transition. And instead of trying to convince the whole world to eat less meat, maybe we can remake meat instead.

Recent findings suggest that nick Petrić Howe: Continuing my theme of small confessions throughout this series. I have another. I love meat.

I like cooking it. I like the smell of it. Most of all, I like to eat it. Now, maybe that doesn’t sound like much of a confession — I’m in good company, most people around the world eat meat to some degree. But, if you know the environmental concerns around meat, then you’ll know why this is a confession.

According to recent reports, basically, meat leads to a lot more carbon emissions than the alternative of eating plants or plant-based products. That comes down to simple physics. Animals eat plants, and then we eat the animals. Energy is lost through that process and so it is less efficient that you and I just going straight to the source of that energy — eating the plants themselves that have captured the sun’s light. There's a bit more to it than that, but on the face of it eating meat is just less efficient than eating a plant.

That inefficiency leads to warming emissions, with the world Food and Agricultural Organisation (the FAO) estimating that around 15% of global emissions coming from livestock.

It has been revealed that and as someone growing up worrying about the climate, I knew this and became a vegetarian because of it. I kept it up through most of my twenties, somewhat successfully. There was the occasional burger I must admit, as like I mentioned, I love meat, so this wasn’t an easy life choice to make. In fact it was so hard that, after losing some weight to an illness, I stopped.

Industry observers note that now I eat meat sparingly, but I do still eat it. Something that I feel guilty about. So, when I got an email about a book suggesting that rather than trying to change how much humans love meat we could change the way it’s produced to cut its climate cost, my interest was piqued.

Bruce Friedrich: In the book, I focus on plant-based meat and cultivated meat.

This is Bruce Fredreich, the founder of the Global Food Institute, a climate nonprofit that seeks to figure out how to make alternatives to meat.

According to recent reports, bruce Friedrich: And the idea of plant-based meat is to say, look, meat is made up of fats, proteins, minerals, and water. Plants also have fats, proteins, minerals, and water. What would it look like to use science to reconstitute plants such that they were indistinguishable from animal meat? And then with cultivated meat, really is as simple as let's take the science of tissue engineering, apply it to meat, which means we can have food grade systems, food grade ingredients, food grade manufacturing and scale it up.

Recent findings suggest that nick Petrić Howe: I’ll hasten to point out that Bruce is the first to admit that this isn’t that simple, but he makes the case that it can be done, and we are getting closer to that. And if we can get the costs down, then he thinks many people would happily switch to eat these alternatives to meat. Recent polling backs him up. Nearly half of Britons between the ages of 16 and 29 say they would eat lab grown meat — those numbers do decline as people get older, but they point to a common theme. Generally younger people are more willing to eat cultivated or plant-based meat and nearly two thirds of Americans say they would be willing to reduce their meat consumption — even though that consumption has stayed the same so far.

So, the willingness may be there. According to Bruce, if we give people alternatives that taste just as good and are as cheap, if not cheaper than meat, that willingness may finally cause the dietary shift that climate scientists have long hoped for. That’s the significant idea that Bruce has dedicated the past decade to. On founding the Global Food Institute he’s been dedicated to figuring out how to make alternative meats that taste and cost the same as the original.

Recent findings suggest that now, if you follow the science of alternative meats, you may be feeling a little sceptical. I know I was. As much as I wanted to believe in what Bruce was telling me, I feel like I’ve heard that cultivated meat has been about 10 years away for a long time now, and while plant-based meat is more mature — you can go buy it in the supermarket — it doesn’t really taste like meat.

Bruce acknowledges that there are challenges, but he’s optimistic.

Bruce Friedrich: Well I mean I think we overcome the big challenges in the same way that we overcome any other big challenge that's based in science, which is as many people as possible focused on solving the key challenges that we're going to have to solve to get to taste and price parity. That's going to be true on the plant-based side. It's also going to be true on the cultivated side. I talk about this in the book, but one of the things I found most surprising is that the challenge of cultivated meat is significantly more straightforward than the challenge of plant-based meat. The challenge of plant-based meat, it's difficult to get plant fats and proteins to behave like animal fats and proteins. And all over the world, any place you've got a tissue engineering department at a university or anybody working on tissue engineering, all of those people have the basic skill set to solve the cultivated meat scientific challenges. But up until a decade ago, nobody had really tried to figure out how to make plant fats and proteins behave like animal fats and proteins. There's just not another use case for it other than plant-based meat. So it might be scientifically, I mean, it might be scientifically simpler, but there are far fewer people working on the challenge. So in the book, I talk about the fact that we need to change that.

According to recent reports, nick Petrić Howe: With enough people working on the problem, Bruce thinks we can solve it. Maybe not tomorrow, or even soon, but it certainly is possible. But to get enough people working on the problem we have to talk about the dreaded F word. Funding.

In a recent development, on that though, Bruce points out that in recent years governments have started taking quite a lot of notice of this. But they're not typically motivated by climate concerns, instead they're looking to create a cheaper and more reliable food system.

It has been revealed that bruce Friedrich: And this just makes intuitive sense. If you want to raise a chicken for food — and chickens are the most efficient animals at turning crops into meat — it's going to take you in your best-case scenario about nine calories fed to a chicken to get one calorie back out from the chicken. And what that means is that for countries that do not have high food self-sufficiency ratios, they are importing vast amounts of feed crops and they're importing a lot of meat. This is particularly true for China, which when it joined the WTO about 25 years ago was food self-sufficient. Now its food self-sufficiency ratio is down around 70 % and they don't like that. They do not want to be dependent on a global marketplace to feed themselves. This is even more true for countries like Korea, Japan, Singapore, Israel, that are even smaller and have even lower food self-sufficiency ratios. And that and the economic benefits is the reason that governments are enthusiastic about this intervention.

Nick Petrić Howe:This taps a little into what Hannah was saying earlier. One way to tackle climate change is to combine with other problems. Here, promoting self-sufficiency may make governments take notice, and it would come with a climate co-benefit. This isn’t the only advantage of these alt meats.

Industry observers note that one of science’s greatest challenges, apart from climate change, is antimicrobial resistance. This is where things like bacteria, viruses and fungi become resistant to he medicines we have to fight them. And meat is not innocent here either.

Antibiotics are often given to healthy animals as it can promote their growth, but this is the exact kind of overuse of antibiotics that scientists have long been warning against as it can lead to antimicrobial resistance.

Bruce suggests that alternative meats, by cutting out animals from the production, could avoid this particular ticking time bomb. Also, for people who worry about the morality of eating animals, having a tasty alternative grown from cells or plants, could help them have their meat and eat it too.

But there are some major hurdles to overcome, before we're all tucking in to our fake meat of choice. Currently, lab-grown meat is prohibitively expensive. And plant-based meat has been tricky to make taste like the real thing, which may put some would-be consumers off. Bruce acknowledges that there’s a far way to go, but he also points to the progress that’s already been made. In 2013, the first lab-grown meat burger was eaten. That cost Sergey Brin, one of Google’s cofounders, 250,000 euros, or around 330,000 US dollars. Today, you can buy cultivated salmon on bagel in Portland, Oregon for $24. And Bruce estimates that a cultivated burger would cost around twice the price of a regular one. As prices tumble, Bruce hopes it’ll encourage more people — vegetarians and meat lovers both — to eat alternative proteins.

In a recent development, he likens the challenge of reimagining meat to that of the energy transition. With enough effort to make a tasty and cheap alternative, more and more people will make the switch.

Recent findings suggest that bruce Friedrich: So I just find it remarkable that there have been multiple journalists, smart people, who have written about plant-based meat that because it is still too expensive and not good enough, it has failed. As though because we haven't done it yet. We're never ever going to be able to do it. And then uncultivated meat people will say well gosh we put three billion dollars into this. You know where's my cultivated burger? Without thinking about what scientific progress looks like in the context of literally everything else that's ever been done. So three billion dollars across 100 companies and all of time, which is a decade, that's not very long and that's not very much money.

#25230. Latest Update: Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting

📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (798 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Fact check: Online disinformation rife after Krakow mass shooting

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (798 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police.
  • On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office confirmed a formal investigation.
  • Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media customers to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A gunman killed six people in a shooting spree in Krakow's Old Town on Saturday, before being shot and detained by police. The gunman, who is also suspected of killing three family members before the attack, later died in hospital.

On Monday, Poland's national prosecutor's office confirmed a formal investigation.

Nevertheless, much is still unknown about the details of the crime, leaving social media customers to fill the information vacuum with fake images of the attacker and alleged screenshots of his online profile. DW Fact Check breaks down the developing story.

Claim: A viral picture has been circulating on social media claiming to be the real image of the suspected attacker.

In the post, the image is posted with the caption, "[…] The perpetrator of the attack in Krakow is a 25-year-old Polish citizen, Polish police have reported. The death toll has reached six. (…)".

But the unusual sharpness of this picture raises doubt of its authenticity. It is difficult to imagine capturing such a clear image in a chaotic situation.

DW checked the image using two different AI detectors. Hive Moderation identified it as 99.5% AI-generated, while Google's SynthID Detector confirmed that it contains a SynthID watermark, indicating that it was generated or edited using Google's AI technology.

In our research we found several versions of the suspect image circulating online, most looking very similar. We also found a number of images and videos showing the attack.

Although DW cannot independently verify the footage, it shares similarities in terms of the people and background with some original images published by picture agencies.

It appears the AI-generated images may have been created using this footage as a reference. Some of the posts sharing these images have also been labeled as AI-generated.

One notable thing to understand is that AI cannot sharpen a blurry image with correct details or recover details that are not visible in an original photograph. It can generate plausible details based on the surrounding visual information, but these are essentially guesses, not exact reproductions of what was actually there.

More about this and how customers used sharpening AI tools here.

Claim: "Michal Oksinski, the terrorist from Krakow who also killed his parents and sister, had a Telegram account with the Ukrainian flag. On November 3, he wrote 'Thanks, Dad, for the gun', posting this photo of himself wearing the Ukrainian flag insignia," an X user wrote in a post viewed more than 700,000 times.

This Telegram channel is almost certainly inauthentic. The account allegedly posted a photo on November 3, showing the attacker holding a gun, standing in front of a television and a Ukrainian insignia on the wall.

According to recent reports, another post on November 4 simply reads, "11/7/2026", the date of the attack. Both of these posts were edited on November 8, after the suspect had been apprehended.

DW verified on the Telegram app by hovering over the posts to show the edit history. The channel's photo, a Ukrainian flag, was also edited after the attack took place.

This is a common disinformation tactic — fake accounts will edit old posts and pictures in the days after a breaking news event to give the appearance that they've predicted or announced the event in advance.

In a recent development, further proof: in Poland, the date is written first, not the month. And the photo of the alleged attacker itself is almost certainly AI-generated. HIVE Moderation noted it was 99.9% likely to be created with AI.

According to recent reports, claim: "#BREAKING: The attacker in Poland had a full arsenal in this trunk! He also has forward observation group patches, an American military firm active in Ukraine," reads an X post viewed nearly 100,000 times. The attached photo of the supposed "arsenal" in the trunk has been shared by several other accounts.

The attached photo claims to show the attacker's car with a trunk full of guns, ammunition, a helmet and a military vest.

The vest in the trunk of the car features a symbol supposedly connected to the Forward Observations Group, an American tactical training lifestyle brand that has traveled to and operated in Ukraine.

The patch, however, is the Old Roger flag, a symbol commonly used in military circles. The Forward Observations Group logo is a variation of this symbol, featuring a horned skeleton holding a gun, not an hourglass.

It has been revealed that this is also not the attacker's car from the scene of the crime. This license plate is registered with the Krakow police, indicating they likely collected evidence from the crime scene and moved it to this car.

Little details like these can help separate fact from fiction, especially in a rapidly evolving story like the Krakow shooting.

Daniel Ebertz contributed to this article.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paulo Dybala and Mile Svilar are expected to be back in the starting XI for Roma when they face Parma on Saturday, after one and two months out of action respectively.

The break for international duty closes and Serie A returns this weekend with the Week 12 fixtures, and the Giallorossi take on Parma on Saturday at 17.00 GMT (18.00 CET).

The good news for coach Gian Piero Gasperini is that the treatment room is finally starting to empty out after an injury crisis.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall believes Thierno Barry's impressive form for Everton is the product of relentless work to improve his game behind the scenes.

Barry has notched 13 goal involvements (10 goals, three assists) in all competitions so far this season, most recently a quick-fire brace in the Blues' 3-1 come-from-behind victory over Coventry City prior to the international break.

The French striker also produced the assist for Dewsbury-Hall's goal against Frank Lampard's side – and it comes as no surprise to the Toffees' No.8 to see his teammate thriving.

"I'm so happy for Thierno," Dewsbury-Hall told evertontv. "He's reaping the rewards for how hard he works. He's on the training pitch every day, working at his game.

"He's playing pretty much every minute for us, at the moment, which is tough in itself.

According to recent reports, "Cream always rises [to the top] when you work hard. I'm a big believer in that.

"I know he'll keep working, keep a level head and I think he'll keep getting better and better, because he's got the right attitude.".

Dewsbury-Hall has also praised the collective mentality of Everton this season.

He added: "[The Coventry game] was another example of us reacting positively to a setback. I think on the night their goal actually kicked us into gear, because it wasn't the best first half from us.

"I thought we reacted unbelievably, though, and we blew them away in the final half hour or so, which was vital to top off a really good week for us.

"We've been in pretty much every game this season, even if we haven't been at our best, which is pleasing.".

Pervis Estupinan has received a great deal of criticism at Milan after the move from Brighton, so there are reports his agent has proposed a potential loan to Fiorentina in January instead.

The Ecuador international was a significant investment at €18m from Brighton and Hove Albion in the summer of 2025, but he never quite managed to deliver on that promise.

There were already calls for him to be sold this season to Aston Villa, only for coach Ruben Amorim to publicly insist he was the one who wanted to keep the player.

According to Sport Mediaset and Firenzeviola, even Amorim has now conceded that Estupinan is out of opportunities at San Siro, and ought to look elsewhere.

It is reported that his agent Jorge Mendes has contacted Fiorentina director Fabio Paratici to suggest a possible loan deal in the January transfer window.

This would also include an option to buy at the end of the season, although it is unlikely the Rossoneri will make back the money spent to sign him.

Estupinan has made 10 appearances for Milan so far this season between Serie A and the Europa League, but only started one of the last five league games.

“Wow, wow, wow,” Harry Kane stated as he took to the stage at the London Palladium after winning the 2026 Ballon d’Or. Wow indeed. “I am speechless,” Kane added before launching into a heartfelt speech, the wobble in his voice showing just how much this meant to him.

Recent findings suggest that in truth it would have been a travesty had the 33-year-old England captain – and Bayern Munich striker – not won with his family, friends and coaches all watching from the stalls at this famous old theatre. “All those years of sacrifice,” he stated of his parents, Pat and Kim, his voice faltering more than ever at that moment. It was from the heart. And faltering again as he spoke about his wife and “best friend” Katie Goodland. “This is a trophy we all celebrate,” he said, talking to his children back in Bavaria. “I bring a few others [trophies] home but this one is a special one.”.

Recent findings suggest that kane’s speech was as outstanding as his football. “Lastly for me it is the journey,” he said. “Learn through resilience, determination and self-belief. My journey was not easy and I had to fight my way to be the very best right now. I hope that can give you inspiration.”.

So much for the “one-season wonder”. So much for the doubters who poured scorn on him. So much for those who believed he would never make it after loan spells at Leyton Orient, Millwall, Norwich City and Leicester City. With varying degrees of success.

Sources indicate that kate Scott, the presenter, perfectly detected the emotion and remarked: “You held it together. You got through it.” It demonstrated how much it meant to Kane, who simply and quietly replied: “Yes”.

What a winner. What a player. What a role model. The award given in the city where he has scored most of his goals. But he would not have been in the running for this accolade had he not been brave enough to quit Tottenham Hotspur after 19 years and move to Germany.

According to recent reports, kane was the favourite. But, despite its prestige, the Ballon d’Or process is an odd one. One journalist from each of the top-100-ranked Fifa countries is given a vote, with the organisers, France Football, laying out the criteria: individual performance, collective performance and fair play. In that order. They often go for the biggest name. Not the best.

Kane’s numbers are incredible. They speak for themselves. Those numbers show he deserved to win the prize: 65 games for club and country and 73 goals. Plus eight assists (for the judging period – August 3, 2025 to July 19, 2026). That is 61 goals for Bayern and 12 for England. That is a goal less than every 72 minutes. That is beyond elite. That is world class and legendary.

He reached his century of Bundesliga goals last month in just 98 games, destroying Dieter Müller’s record set 49 years ago – he took 129 matches.

Kane became one of only two players in history (the other is Ronaldo) to score 20-plus goals across World Cups and European Championships and was the only one to score in two major club cup finals, including a hat-trick. Those are the facts, but there is also the football and, yes, the conduct. Kane has scored some superb goals during that period, not least for England. The Prince of Wales, who has been FA president since 2006, congratulated Kane on “a fantastic achievement”.

And he is often seen winning as many defensive headers in his own penalty area as attacking ones in the opposition’s.

It has been revealed that that work extends to off the pitch, to try to maximise his ability, to do everything to be the best version of himself and to be the best. Which he has now been recognised as. And it stems from his winning mentality. Some scoffed when Kane walked into England’s press conference before the 2018 World Cup and remarked he could be top-scorer – but he proved them wrong.

In a recent development, they probably also scoffed at the notion that he would one day be declared the best player in the world and win the Ballon d’Or. But he has done all that. It confirms England’s all-time cap holder (for now jointly with Peter Shilton) and goalscorer as one of the greats. And we are privileged to witness that greatness. Wow, what a night.

By Christian FalkGermany do not have a single player among the 30 in the running to win the Ballon d’Or in London on Monday night – but Bayern Munich do have England captain Harry Kane.

According to recent reports, for the 35-time German champions, the award is perhaps even more crucial than it is for the peerless striker himself. The Bayern hierarchy are planning to travel to the Palladium Theatre en masse to support Kane.

Recent findings suggest that kane is not only Bayern’s top striker, he is their international figurehead and, internally, their poster-boy professional. Club patron and honorary president Uli Hoeness described the England captain as the best signing in the club’s history. Hoeness even went so far as to say he loves Kane, and he is not alone in this.

Recent findings suggest that there's only one Harry Kane. https://t.co/NfZEFmjaUN.

Recent findings suggest that hoeness is one of many in the club’s leadership who have been endlessly promoting Kane to help the 33-year-old fulfil his lifelong dream of winning the trophy. Bayern officials have been campaigning on his behalf for weeks.

According to recent reports, first up was manager Vincent Kompany, who remains in hospital for tests after collapsing at Bayern’s training ground on Friday. Kompany said: “If he can now crown his career or his season with the Ballon d’Or, that would be fitting given the way he plays for the team.”.

The plaudits kept coming. Whether it was sporting director Max Eberl (“He has more than earned the Ballon d’Or. Anyone who loves football loves characters like Harry Kane”), chief executive Jan-Christian Dreesen (“One thing is clear – anyone talking about this year’s greatest individual honours cannot overlook Harry Kane”) or president Herbert Hainer (“Harry Kane embodies the idea that sporting greatness is incomplete without greatness of character. He would be a worthy World Footballer of the Year”), everyone at the club is fighting for Kane.

The official Ballon d’Or website has confirmed Harry Kane, Kylian Mbappe and Lamine Yamal as winners of the main prize in an embarrassing blunder for the organisation.

Three separate articles were published before quickly being taken down.

The headline on Kane’s article read: ‘Harry Kane wins 2026 Ballon d’Or: Here are his best and most meaningful strikes from a 61-goal season’.

According to recent reports, the 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony takes place at the London Palladium as England and Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane aims to become the first Englishman in more than 20 years to win the award. Michael Owen was the last Englishman to win the award back in 2001.

The choice of London as the host city pays tribute to the award’s inaugural winner, England’s Stanley Matthews, who won it in 1956. This also marks the first time the ceremony will be organised outside France. Kane, who scored over 70 goals for club and country in the relevant year, is among the favourites for this year’s award alongside the likes of Barcelona and Spain’s Lamine Yamal and Real Madrid and France’s Kylian Mbappe.

Industry observers note that kane won the Bundesliga with Bayern Munich whereas Yamal won both La Liga and the World Cup. Yamal won the Kopa Trophy at last year’s ceremony as the best men’s young player.

Recent findings suggest that last year’s winners were Spain and Barcelona midfielder Aitana Bonmati and France and Barcelona forward Ousmane Dembele. Dembele is aiming to become just the 11th man to win the top prize at least twice, although it would appear to be very unlikely that the Frenchman will be winning the award this evening.

Selected international journalists cast their votes based on the performances of players throughout the season. The panel consists of one representative per country from the top 100 nations in the Fifa men’s world ranking and the top 50 in the women’s world ranking. Each voter ranks their top 10 candidates, with points distributed on a descending scale. They vote based on three factors: individual performance, team achievements, and class combined with fair play.

Sources indicate that in total, 13 trophies will be presented across the men’s and women’s game, including the two man Ballon d’Or awards, the best young players and best teams. The awards take into account achievements from August 3, 2025, to July 19, 2026 (August 16 for the women).

The official ceremony begins at 8pm GMT.

Borussia Dortmund's Felix Nmecha and the question of religion

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (848 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.
  • According to recent reports, "Faith does not justify exclusion.
  • "In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Felix Nmecha's renewed use of the "Crowns down celebration" — where a crown is pretended to be removed from someone's head and placed at Jesus' feet — has sparked a reaction from Borussia Dortmund's official supporters' group.

According to recent reports, "Faith does not justify exclusion. Faith does not justify division. Borussia Dortmund is a club for everyone," read a statement after the Bundesliga club beat Elversberg, a game in which Nmecha scored twice. Nmecha's first documented "Crowns down celebration" was at the 2026 World Cup, for which "The King's Return" campaign was launched.

"In the past, the the Borussia Dortmund supporters club has deliberately refrained from commenting on sports-related issues and the athletic performance of individual players. We remain committed to this approach," the statement continued.

"However, when it comes to our club's values, discrimination, and the question of what view of humanity is fostered within and around Borussia Dortmund, we cannot and will not remain silent.".

The fan club states their issue is not with Nmecha being a devout Christian, but rather his public support for "The King's Return" campaign, which the supporters club stated "gives us cause to reassess the situation.".

This campaign, according to research by German public broadcaster ARD in the summer of 2026, was designed by the "Ballers in God" (MASSIVE) network. BIG was founded in 2015 by footballer John Bostock, a devout Christian who wanted to create a community where professional footballers could strengthen each other in their faith, pray together, and read the Bible. In over a decade since, the BIG community has grown to nearly 800,000 followers on Instagram.

Nmecha issued a response on social media not long afterwards, writing:.

"I've been told that my most recent goal celebration has led to some misunderstandings," Nmecha wrote.

In a recent development, "My message was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form. As Christians, our message is one of love and respect for every person—regardless of where someone comes from, what they believe in, or what worldview they hold.".

Reports suggest that both the board at Dortmund and Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp will speak to Nmecha on the matter in the coming days.

The fan club say their criticism is "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalized because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices... When religious beliefs are used to deny people their dignity or equality, that is where our tolerance for intolerance ends.".

It has been revealed that here, they are referring to the recent ARD investigation. That work revealed the homepage for "The King's Return" campaign featured a link to a live counseling chat run by US-based evangelical nonprofit Groundwire. During the investigations, counselors told reporters that abortion is "Satan's strategy" and that homosexuality is a sin.

Borussia Dortmund's statement of core values commits the club to diversity, human rights, and inclusion regardless of gender, sexual orientation, faith, or background. The club's largest and most influential fan group also promotes progressive, anti-fascist, and inclusive values. It is also part of a wider fan landscape in Germany where club members are more involved in club decisions than in many other countries. This was evidenced when the club signed a deal with arms manufacturer Rheinmetall two years ago and in the case of Nmecha as well. When the midfielder signed for Dortmund in 2023, many of the club's fans protested because the player had previously shared or liked several transphobic and homophobic posts on his Instagram account. In response, Nmecha deleted some posts and instead issued a statement emphasizing "I do not discriminate against anyone.".

Recent findings suggest that article 4 of German Basic Law guarantees that each individual is allowed to decide how strongly, why and which god to believe in. In football, players cannot display political, religious, or personal slogans, statements, or images on their jerseys, undershirts, or gear. However, physical gestures are allowed so long as they don't delay the game or antagonize the crowd.

The use of physical religious gestures has history in sports, as professor Paul Putz described in his book "The Spirit of the Game: American Christianity and Big-Time Sports". Putz describes how the the pioneers of the Christian athlete movement realized they: "could influence others to Christian ideals more effectively on the field than in the pulpit.".

And yet, such gestures can also be at odds with the atmosphere of modern sports arenas, particularly football. In their book "Sports and Christianity: Historical and Contemporary Perspectives", Nick J. Watson and Andrew Parker explain how modern sport has become a substitute for traditional faith.

"Sport seduces the teeming 'global village'; it is the fresh opiate of the masses; it is one of the great modern experiences … Sport, for many, has replaced religion as a source of emotional catharsis and spiritual passion," they wrote.

With the 26-year-old Nmecha a key player for both club and country, the conversation around faith and football looks set to continue for some time yet.

The Norway international remains one of the world’s most prolific forwards, but uncertainty around City’s future has fuelled growing speculation that a departure could become realistic in 2027.

Real Madrid, Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain are also monitoring developments, meaning Liverpool would face extraordinary competition if Haaland genuinely becomes available.

According to Fichajes, Man City could be prepared to negotiate Haaland’s departure for around €150million, roughly £125m, at the end of the season.

According to recent reports, for Liverpool, the attraction is obvious. Haaland already understands the Premier League and would provide an elite focal point capable of transforming any attack immediately.

However, the Reds already have significant investment tied up in their forward line, meaning a move of this magnitude would almost certainly require major departures first.

From Liverpool’s perspective, this would be one of the most ambitious transfers imaginable.

Haaland combines devastating movement, physical power and a goalscoring record few players can match. Adding him to Andoni Iraola’s squad would immediately strengthen Liverpool’s chances of competing for every major trophy.

City remain in a strong contractual position and that Haaland has recently described himself as “incredibly happy” at the Etihad.

Liverpool also have to consider whether spending £125m-plus on one player is compatible with the rest of their squad planning.

Still, if City’s circumstances change and Haaland genuinely becomes available, Liverpool should absolutely explore the possibility.

Players of this calibre almost never reach the market. The challenge would be convincing Haaland that Anfield, rather than Madrid, Barcelona or Paris, should be his next destination.

Italy coach Roberto Mancini sent out a statement following the Nations League elimination. ‘We are on the right track. We will be stronger in March’ when going into the EURO 2028 qualifiers.

The Azzurri had a rollercoaster of a Nations League campaign, as they started with a 2-0 home defeat to Belgium that had some fearing for potential relegation into League B.

That was followed by back-to-back wins over Turkiye, a 1-1 draw in Paris, and stunning 3-1 victory at San Siro over France to go top of the group.

However, a 4-1 loss in Belgium on Sunday saw them finish third and fail to reach the quarter-finals.

“Well done lads,” wrote Mancini on his Instagram account with a picture of him standing with the players in training.

“Despite the disappointment of elimination, we are on the right track. Congratulations to the youngsters.

“We will be stronger in March.”.

A post shared by Roberto Mancini (@mrmancini10).

That is when Italy will next have competitive fixtures, as they head into the European Championship qualifiers.

When Mancini took the job, his second stint on the Azzurri bench after winning the EURO 2020 trophy, he said that the real target was not the Nations League, but to be ready for the European Championship in 2028.

By JOHN MCGARRY, SCOTTISH CHIEF SPORTS FEATURE WRITER.

Published: 17:30 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 17:38 EST, 17 November 2026.

Andy Robertson notes he fully understands why the Tartan Army are increasingly concerned about where the team are going under Sebastien Pocognoli.

Monday’s heavy defeat to Switzerland marked the conclusion of a dismal Nations League campaign which saw the Belgian’s men beat only North Macedonia across six matches to finish a distant third.

After the high of qualifying for the World Cup a year ago, supporters have been brought crashing back to earth since the summer with signs of progress proving hard to come by under the fresh manager.

When the full-time whistle blew in St Gallen to confirm a 4-0 loss, there were audible jeers from the travelling fans.

Skipper Robertson has no problem with what he heard and knows the players have a job on their hands to turn the situation round.

‘I can understand why they’re concerned. I can understand why they’re frustrated,’ he said. ‘I can understand why the away fans didn’t really want us to go over and applaud them.

Robertson can't hide anguish after 4-0 loss on what was his record breaking 103rd cap.

‘I can completely understand that. I’ve been around a long time now and unfortunately I’ve had these nights a couple of times where the fans do react like that.

According to recent reports, ‘You have to let them do that and you also understand why they’re doing it. But I suppose if we’re trying to flip a positive on it, I think maybe the first five or six games under Steve Clarke were maybe similar where we had a lot of change in the squad, we were trying to build something, we were trying to integrate newly introduced people into a new squad and things like that.

Sources indicate that ‘We’re trying to do that and we have to be positive about that. We need the young lads to feel comfortable around us. We need them to step up.

‘We need the older players to really help them in that and really, really step up. And that’s the only way we’re going to be successful.

In a recent development, ‘We’ll still be positive because that’s the only way we know, and we know we can build something special. We’ve done it. We’ve been questioned a few times and bounced back and now we’re going to need to do it again with a newer squad.’.

Robertson admits that the adverse results have fed into a lack of harmony behind the scenes — a sharp contrast to the positivity which was palpable as the side qualified for the World Cup a year ago today.

Robertson understands why fans booed another dismal performance by Pocognoli's team.

‘I still think we need to work on it,’ he mentioned. ‘We still need to get closer as a group again because — I don’t like looking at the past any more — but under Steve we had a really close-knit group where what we created was pretty special.

It has been revealed that ‘And that’s rare but we also have to try and do that again and we’re trying to make the fresh players and the young lads feel as comfortable as possible. That’s the role of the older players and we have to keep doing that.

‘We have to keep encouraging them because they’re the ones that want to take us forward in years to come and they’re also the ones that are going to help us now.

‘Us older lads, we need to put a lot of responsibility on (ourselves) to try and help them do that, to try and keep pushing them, and we have to keep stepping up as well.

‘As a collective, we all need to step up more and if we do that then hopefully we can be successful again.’.

While the spotlight has largely fallen on the manager for persisting with a 3-4-2-1 formation, Robertson is adamant that it’s only fair the blame is shared around.

‘We all have to take responsibility,’ he remarked. ‘Tactics and the way the manager sets us up and everything like that is one thing but then you’ve got 11  players, and we had 16 players, who have to go out and perform.

Skipper Robertson roars with anger and disbelief as Scotland team crumbles in Switzerland.

Industry observers note that ‘I don’t think we performed as a collective good enough. When you get beat 4-0, there’s not going to be any positives. There’s no fan in this stadium that’s going to go home and go: “We played well in the first half”.

‘That’s not how football works and we’re very aware of that. I’m very aware of that in terms of I don’t take any positives from a 4-0 defeat. I’m sorry but that’s the way I am and unfortunately that’s the way it is.’.

The Tottenham man became Scotland’s most capped player on Monday when he pulled on the jersey for the 103rd time, but that achievement was scant consolation at the time.

‘I’ve not given myself the chance to reflect,’ insisted Robertson. ‘In a couple of days’ time, probably when I unlock my phone and I get a couple of messages, I’ll realise what I’ve achieved and I don’t take it for granted.

It has been revealed that ‘I don’t take the magnitude of it for granted either, being able to overtake the legend of Kenny Dalglish. But it’s very hard to focus on myself after a result like that. I always focus on the team first and that’s always been my way.’.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The skulls of a human (left) and a Neanderthal (right).Credit: Philippe Psaila/Science Photo Library.
  • Sources indicate that A genetic variant that seems to reduce the size of brain areas involved in visual processing comes from an unexpected source — Neanderthals.
  • Industry observers note that geneticists have previously found fragments of Neanderthal DNA in the genomes of many modern humans, suggesting that the two species interbred in the millennia before Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The skulls of a human (left) and a Neanderthal (right).Credit: Philippe Psaila/Science Photo Library.

Sources indicate that A genetic variant that seems to reduce the size of brain areas involved in visual processing comes from an unexpected source — Neanderthals. People who carry the variant also have a reduced risk of schizophrenia.

Industry observers note that geneticists have previously found fragments of Neanderthal DNA in the genomes of many modern humans, suggesting that the two species interbred in the millennia before Neanderthals died out about 40,000 years ago. But this variant, described in a study published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences USA today1, has an unusually powerful effect on brain anatomy.

In a recent development, “This is a very important variant,” says computational biologist Davide Marnetto at the University of Turin, Italy. “Its effect is really one of the most beautiful and strong that I’ve ever seen.”.

According to recent reports, when it comes to their brains, humans and Neanderthals have many subtle anatomical differences. Neanderthal brains were more oblong and elongated front to back, whereas modern human brains are rounder. Neanderthals also tended to have slightly larger occipital lobes — the region at the back of the brain that processes visual information.

Neanderthal-like ‘mini-brains’ created in lab with CRISPR.

Neanderthal-like ‘mini-brains’ created in lab with CRISPR.

In their study, evolutionary geneticists Hugo Zeberg and Svante Pääbo at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig, Germany, compared ancient DNA with data from the 1000 Genomes Project and UK BioBank, among other sources. They found evidence that a genetic variant that influences the volume of modern humans’ occipital lobes was inherited from Neanderthals.

In a recent development, zeberg and Pääbo identified the variant in all five detailed Neanderthal genomes that are available to scientists, but found that it is not present in genomes of Denisovans, another extinct hominin group. In modern humans, the variant only occurs in people with non-African ancestry. It is unlikely to have been inherited from an older species that is ancestral to both humans and Neanderthals because it is found in a chunk of DNA that is 59.7 kilobases long — too significant to have survived for hundreds of thousands of years.

“This is a piece of DNA that looks like it comes from Neanderthals,” says Zeberg.

Recent findings suggest that the variant itself is a deletion of four nucleotides on chromosome 14 and was originally identified in 20192. Its effect on people’s brains is the opposite of what might be expected, say Zeberg and Pääbo. Even though Neanderthals had larger occipital lobes than humans do, this Neanderthal-derived variant is associated with a decrease in the volume of a part of the occipital lobe called the cuneus. Each copy of the variant was associated with 0.85 cubic centimetres less volume — an effect on the cuneus larger than that of any other known variant.

The injured were being taken to hospitals in nearby cities, while authorities dispatched two aircraft carrying medical teams and stretcher equipment.

The campaign aimed to support LGBTQ+ rights and foster inclusivity among fans and young people.

After over a decade of collaboration, the league will now lead its own campaign, timed to coincide with LGBTQ+ History Month in February, The Telegraph report.

"Rainbow Laces has benefited from a wide range of partners with a natural ebb and flow reflecting cultural and sporting changes," a Stonewall spokesperson told BBC Sport.

"Alongside other sporting bodies the FA has been instrumental in advancing LGBTQ+ inclusion at the grassroots level and more recently the Women's Super League has taken up the mantle as the women's game has grown - enabling Rainbow Laces to reach more diverse audiences.".

The 26-year-old has enhanced his reputation with a series of outstanding performances for club and country, attracting attention from Chelsea and Juventus. His versatility is particularly appealing, with Araújo capable of operating as a left-back, wing-back or further forward.

For Chelsea, that flexibility would make him an interesting addition to Xabi Alonso’s squad, but Sporting are under no pressure to negotiate midway through the campaign.

According to A BOLA, Chelsea and Juventus have continued gathering information on Araújo in recent months and could potentially make approaches.

However, Sporting’s position is described as absolute: they will not entertain negotiations in January.

Araújo has further increased his value with Uruguay, scoring an impressive six goals in his last seven international appearances. Sporting now consider him one of their most valuable assets and are expected to demand a fee close to his €80million release clause if talks take place next summer.

The Portuguese champions are also preparing for the possibility of eventually losing him, with teenager Moncef Zekri viewed internally as a potential long-term successor.

Araújo offers the intensity, athleticism and attacking contribution required from a modern wide defender, while his ability to cover several roles would give Alonso valuable tactical flexibility.

The Blues have already explored the possibility of signing him before. Chelsea held positive discussions regarding Araújo during the summer, demonstrating that their interest is more than speculative.

It has been revealed that but January is clearly the wrong time to force the matter. Araújo signed an improved Sporting contract until 2030 in August, giving the Portuguese club considerable leverage. His exceptional international form has only strengthened their negotiating position.

Chelsea therefore risk paying significantly above market value if they attempt to change Sporting’s mind this winter.

Waiting until the summer would be far more sensible. By then, Chelsea can reassess their left-sided options and Sporting may be more willing to negotiate.

Araújo is certainly worth monitoring, but paying close to €80m simply to overcome a January refusal would be difficult to justify.

Liverpool, Manchester City and more have also been tracking him, but now teamTALK claim Chelsea have surged to the front of the pack.

According to Spanish newspaper Sport, this is because Barcelona coach Flick has increasing doubts over whether Bastoni would fit into his tactical system.

Although the Italian has played in a four-man defence for the Azzurri under Roberto Mancini, and was watched by Chelsea scouts doing so in the 3-1 victory over France last week, he is still far more suited to three at the back.

This has prompted Flick to pour cold water over Barcelona’s interest, letting Chelsea into the race.
